front: [Chain: SIMM_IM 1/3] Netting set with two sensitivity-based risk factors, weighted sensitivities \(WS_1=10\)m and \(WS_2=-6\)m, correlation \(\rho=0.3\). Using a SIMM-style quadratic aggregation \(IM=\sqrt{s^\top R s}\), what is the initial margin, and what does the cross term do?
back:
Steps:
  1. \(s^\top R s = 10^2 + (-6)^2 + 2(0.3)(10)(-6) = 100+36-36 = 100\).
  2. \(IM = \sqrt{100} = 10\)m.
Undiversified sum of absolute sensitivities is 16m. The cross term is negative because the two sensitivities have opposite signs and are positively correlated, so the offset lowers IM.
Interviewer follow-up: Why does a sign-offsetting trade cut IM even when the net delta of the set is unchanged? (IM is a norm of the sensitivity vector, not a linear function of it, so the cross term carries the offset.)

front: [Chain: SIMM_IM 2/3] Same netting set, \(s=(10,-6)\)m, \(\rho=0.3\), \(IM_0=10\)m. A new trade adds \(a=(0,+4)\)m of weighted sensitivity. What is the exact new IM, what does the first-order (Euler) estimate give, and why do they differ?
back:
Steps:
  1. Exact: \(q=(s+a)^\top R(s+a)=100+2\,a^\top Rs+a^\top Ra=100-24+16=92\), so \(IM_1=\sqrt{92}=9.592\)m. Change \(=-0.408\)m.
  2. Euler estimate: \(\partial IM/\partial\varepsilon=a^\top R s/IM_0=(-12)/10=-1.2\)m, giving \(IM\approx 8.80\)m.
The first-order estimate overstates the reduction by about 0.8m because it drops the \(a^\top R a=16\) term. The second-order term is the same order as the first-order effect here.
Where it breaks: Euler allocation is valid only for small trades. Large hedge trades need a full re-run of the aggregation, and SIMM bucket floors and concentration thresholds add further non-linearity.
Interviewer follow-up: Which marginal IM should the desk charge in MVA on a new trade? (The incremental full re-run, not the Euler derivative.)

front: [Chain: SIMM_IM 3/3] The offsetting trade in the previous card reduces IM by 0.408m at \(t=0\). Estimate the MVA benefit if that reduction were held flat for 5 years, with posting spread \(s_F=80\)bp and flat \(r=3\%\). State what the estimate ignores.
back:
Steps:
  1. Annuity: \(\int_0^5 e^{-0.03t}\,dt=(1-e^{-0.15})/0.03=4.643\).
  2. Benefit \(\approx s_F\times 0.408\times 4.643=0.008\times0.408\times4.643=0.0152\)m, about £15k.
This is an order-of-magnitude figure, not a valuation. A real MVA needs the expected IM profile \(E[IM(t)]\) over the life of the trade, under the funding measure, with the reduction recomputed at each node.
Where it breaks: The IM reduction decays as the underlying trades run off and the netting set's state evolves. A flat t=0 reduction overstates or understates the benefit depending on the profile shape.
Interviewer follow-up: Is the MVA of an offsetting trade always a benefit? (No. It can be negative if the trade adds IM in the states where the netting set is most exposed to the funding spread.)

front: [Chain: XVA_PNL 1/3] A CVA desk runs a daily P&L explain for one counterparty. Write the one-day change in CVA as a sum of components. State the sign convention for the bank's P&L, given that CVA is a reserve against counterparty default.
back:
Answer: \(\Delta CVA = \Theta + \sum_x \frac{\partial CVA}{\partial x}\Delta x + \Delta_{exp} + \Delta_{trades} + \Delta_{model} + \varepsilon\), where:
  • \(\Theta\): time roll with market and exposure held fixed.
  • Spread CS01 \(\times\Delta s\), rates delta \(\times\Delta r\), FX delta \(\times\Delta fx\).
  • \(\Delta_{exp}\): re-simulation of the netting set under new market data (exposure and correlation moves that are not a single Greek).
  • \(\Delta_{trades}\): new, amended or matured trades.
  • \(\Delta_{model}\): calibration and methodology changes.
  • \(\varepsilon\): residual, including second-order cross terms.
Bank P&L is \(-\Delta CVA\): a CVA increase is a loss.
Interviewer follow-up: Which component is the diagnostic one? (The residual, scaled by the size of the market moves. Section on residual follows in the stretch card.)

front: [Chain: XVA_PNL 2/3] Netting set with flat expected positive exposure \(EE=3\)m for 5 years, LGD 60%, flat hazard \(\lambda=2\%\) (spread 120bp), flat \(r=3\%\). CVA with a flat hazard is \(LGD\cdot EE\cdot\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+r}\bigl(1-e^{-(\lambda+r)\tau}\bigr)\) for remaining tenor \(\tau\). Compute the CVA and its one-day theta.
back:
Steps:
  1. \(LGD\cdot EE=1.8\)m; \(\lambda/(\lambda+r)=0.02/0.05=0.4\); \(e^{-0.25}=0.7788\).
  2. \(CVA(5)=1.8\times0.4\times(1-0.7788)=0.1593\)m, about £159k.
  3. \(CVA(5-1/252)-CVA(5)\approx -0.000111\)m, so the CVA falls by about £111 per day from roll-down alone. The bank's P&L from theta is about +£111 per day.
Where it breaks: Flat EE and a flat hazard make the CVA curve monotone in \(\tau\). For an at-the-money swap whose EE peaks mid-life, theta over the hump can be positive or negative, so the sign is not guaranteed.
Interviewer follow-up: Is this theta the same as carry? (Not quite. Carry on the hedge also includes CDS running coupon and funding, which are separate lines in the explain.)

front: [Chain: XVA_PNL 3/3] Same CVA book as the previous card, overnight: spread 120bp to 125bp, \(r\) 3.00% to 2.98%, and \(EE\) from 3.0m to 3.1m. The CVA rises by about £11.8k, so the bank's P&L is about -£11.8k. Give the explain and say what the residual means.
back:
Steps: (CVA changes, with bank P&L equal to the negative)
  • Theta: CVA \(-£0.11\)k, P&L \(+£0.11\)k.
  • Spread (+5bp, CS01 about £1.26k/bp; exact 5 x 1.263): CVA \(+£6.32\)k, P&L \(-£6.32\)k.
  • Exposure (EE +0.1m, +3.3%): CVA \(+£5.31\)k, P&L \(-£5.31\)k.
  • Rates (-2bp): CVA \(+£0.08\)k, P&L \(-£0.08\)k.
  • Residual: CVA \(+£0.20\)k, P&L \(-£0.20\)k.
Components are first-order Greeks at the start-of-day book, and the residual is the realised total less their sum. Sum of CVA changes: \(-0.11+6.32+5.31+0.08+0.20=11.80\)k, matching the realised move (exact total \(11.79\)k).
The exposure move is almost as large as the spread move, so the desk must not treat the exposure line as noise. The residual is about 2% of the move and is within tolerance for a single-counterparty book, but a repeat of this size would need checking against the cross-gamma between spread and EE.
Interviewer follow-up: What would you check first if the residual were 20% of the move? (Whether the spread and exposure lines were computed on the same market snapshot, then cross-gammas, then booking.)

front: [Chain: WWR 1/3] Exposure \(V=\sigma Z\) with \(Z\) standard normal. Default occurs when \(X=\rho Z+\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,\varepsilon>k\), with \(\Phi(-k)=p\), i.e. \(k=\Phi^{-1}(1-p)\). Tabulate the conditional-default exposure multiplier \(m(\rho,p)=E[V\mid D]/\sigma=\rho\,\varphi(k)/p\) for \(p\in\{1\%,2\%,5\%\}\), \(\rho\in\{0.25,0.5,0.75\}\), and explain how it behaves as \(p\) falls.
back:
Table (rows \(p\), columns \(\rho=0.25, 0.5, 0.75\)):
  • \(p=1\%\) (\(k=-2.326\)): 0.666, 1.333, 1.999
  • \(p=2\%\) (\(k=-2.054\)): 0.605, 1.210, 1.816
  • \(p=5\%\) (\(k=-1.645\)): 0.516, 1.031, 1.547
Check: \(p=2\%,\rho=0.5\) gives \(m=1.21\), so \(E[V\mid D]=6.05\)m at \(\sigma=5\)m.
The multiplier is linear in \(\rho\). It grows as \(p\) falls because \(\varphi(k)/p\) is the upper-tail inverse Mills ratio, which rises with \(k=\Phi^{-1}(1-p)\) (about 2.33 at 1%, 1.64 at 5%), and \(k\) grows like \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/p)}\) for small \(p\).
Interviewer follow-up: What does this imply for a constant-\(\rho\) model applied to a single-name counterparty with 1% PD? (At \(\rho=1\) the default-state exposure is \(2.67\sigma\), so a constant-\(\rho\) model may understate tail wrong-way risk if \(\rho\) is calibrated on the bulk of the distribution.)

front: [Chain: WWR 2/3] Exposure \(V^+=(Z)^+\) with \(Z\) standard normal, flat 5y CVA, LGD 60%. The counterparty hazard is made state-dependent: \(\lambda=\lambda_0\,e^{bZ-b^2/2}\) with \(\lambda_0=2\%\), so the same \(Z\) drives exposure and default. Quadrature over \(Z\) gives a CVA ratio to the independent case (constant hazard \(\lambda_0\)) of 1.67 for \(b=0.5\) and 2.31 for \(b=1\). Explain the mechanism and why \(E[\lambda]=\lambda_0\) matters.
back:
Mechanism: The CVA is \(LGD\cdot E[V^+(1-S_T)]\), where \(S_T\) is survival. When \(Z\) is high, exposure is high and the hazard is high, so the product is larger than under independence. This is specific wrong-way risk modelled through a shared factor.
Why \(E[\lambda]=\lambda_0\): \(E[e^{bZ-b^2/2}]=1\), so the mean hazard matches the market-implied level. The ratio then isolates the dependence effect, not a change in the average default probability. This is the calibration condition a CVA model should satisfy before WWR is layered on.
Where it breaks: The per-path constant hazard is a crude approximation of a full term structure, and the result depends on \(b\), which needs calibration to a market-implied correlation or to a stress. A single factor also ignores the case where exposure and default are driven by different factors.
Interviewer follow-up: What is the ratio as \(b\to0\)? (It tends to 1: the hazard is then constant, so exposure and default are independent.)

front: [Chain: WWR 3/3] A bank hedges the spread CS01 of a CVA with single-name CDS on the counterparty. Independent CS01 is about £1.26k per bp (from the earlier P&L case). Under the WWR model in the previous card with \(b=0.5\), the spread CS01 is 1.59 times the independent CS01 (the CVA value ratio is 1.67). The hedge CDS has RPV01 of 4.5. Give the hedge notional under WWR and under independence, and state the residual risk.
back:
Steps:
  1. WWR CS01 \(\approx 1.59\times1.26=2.00\)k/bp (quadrature on the lognormal-hazard model, ratio of \(\partial CVA/\partial\lambda_0\)).
  2. Notional \(=\text{CS01}/(\text{RPV01}\times 1\text{bp})=2.00\times10^3/(4.5\times10^{-4})\approx\pounds4.4\)m.
  3. Independent: \(1.26\times10^3/(4.5\times10^{-4})\approx\pounds2.8\)m.
The WWR hedge is about 59% larger. Sizing on unconditional EE under-hedges the spread risk.
Residual risk: The hedge is sized at the current state. Under WWR the optimal hedge ratio moves with the exposure, so it must be rebalanced, and any basis between the counterparty's CDS and its loans or bonds leaves the default-state exposure unhedged.
Interviewer follow-up: Would you use the CDS notional or the CS01 ratio to size the hedge? (Match CS01, because the CDS notional is not the exposure; the CS01 includes the default-state exposure.)

front: [Chain: EXPO_SIM 1/3] A netting set has one fixed cashflow of £1m due on day 10, between simulation nodes at day 5 and day 15. Is the cashflow in the exposure at node day 5? At node day 15? What happens to the EE profile if the grid omits day 10?
back:
Answer: At day 5 the cashflow is a future flow, so it is in the MTM. At day 15 it has been paid and is out of the MTM. Between nodes, the exposure drops by £1m at day 10. If day 10 is not a node, the drop is smeared across the whole interval, so the EE is overstated for days 5 to 10 and understated for days 10 to 15, with the integral error depending on the interval length and the cashflow size.
Convention: Every cashflow date and every collateral-call date should be a simulation node, so that payments and margin transfers show up as jumps at their own times.
Interviewer follow-up: Does a grid that misses payment dates bias the CVA or only the EE profile? (Both, because the CVA integrates EE against the default density. The bias is small when the flow is small relative to the EE, and large for a bullet.)

front: [Chain: EXPO_SIM 2/3] The CVA is \(LGD\int E^{\mathbb Q}\bigl[D(0,t)V_t^+\bigr]\,dF(t)\), where \(F\) is the default distribution. Why can you not simply use the \(t\)-forward measure at each node, and what identity lets you convert a discounted expectation to a forward-measure one?
back:
Identity: \(E^{\mathbb Q}[D(0,t)V_t]=P(0,t)\,E^{t}[V_t]\), where \(E^t\) is the expectation under the \(t\)-forward measure, with \(P(\cdot,t)\) as numeraire. This holds for any \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable payoff, including \(V_t^+\) with the positive part applied under \(E^t\).
Why not per node: The CVA integral needs the joint behaviour of exposures across nodes and the default time, which is a single path. Each node in its own measure gives correct marginal EEs but no consistent path. A spot-measure path with discounting inside, or a consistent multi-measure construction, is required for the integral.
Where it breaks: Under the spot measure the discount factor sits inside the path; mixing measure choices across nodes without the Radon-Nikodym factor gives inconsistent EEs and an invalid CVA integral.
Interviewer follow-up: Give a case where the forward-measure EE is easy. (A linear swap with a single fixed date, where \(V_t\) is a martingale under \(E^t\) and its EE is a Bachelier expression.)

front: [Chain: EXPO_SIM 3/3] A CVA desk computes CS01 by bump-and-revalue on a Monte Carlo CVA. Explain why common random numbers across the base and bumped runs matter, and what goes wrong with a pathwise derivative when the default indicator is in the payoff.
back:
Answer: With common random numbers the same normal draws drive base and bumped valuations, so the difference cancels most of the MC noise and the CS01 standard error is much smaller than the difference of two independent runs.
Pathwise breakdown: The CVA contains an indicator \(1\{\tau\le t\}\) in its default leg. Its derivative with respect to a parameter is zero almost everywhere and a Dirac at the jump. Pathwise differentiation through the default time therefore gives zero or unstable values. Desks handle this by using the survival probability (a smooth function of \(\lambda\)) in the CVA formula, or by a likelihood-ratio or a smoothed default indicator.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is the spread CS01 of a CVA not the same as a pathwise AAD derivative with respect to \(\lambda\)? (AAD differentiates the tape; the default indicator must be smoothed or replaced by survival weights, or AAD gives the wrong sign or zero.)

front: Derivation: Collateral with threshold \(H\) and no MTA or MPoR. The MTM is \(V\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\). Derive the expected uncollateralised exposure \(EE_H=E[(V-H)^+]\) in closed form, then evaluate for \(\mu=0\), \(\sigma=2\)m, \(H=1\)m.
back:
Steps:
  1. Standardise. Let \(m=\mu-H\). Then \(V-H\sim N(m,\sigma^2)\).
  2. Truncated mean. \(E[X^+]\) for \(X\sim N(m,\sigma^2)\) is \(mN(m/\sigma)+\sigma\varphi(m/\sigma)\). Write \(d=m/\sigma\) and \(N,\varphi\) for the standard normal CDF and density.
  3. Evaluate. \(d=-0.5\), \(N(-0.5)=0.3085\), \(\varphi(-0.5)=0.3521\). \(EE_H=(-1)(0.3085)+2(0.3521)=0.3956\)m.
  4. Check. at \(H=0\) the same formula gives \(\sigma\varphi(0)=0.798\)m, matching the direct integral.
Where it breaks: (i) A minimum transfer amount makes the collateral a step function, so the exposure has a dead band of width MTA that this formula ignores. (ii) An MPoR adds a lag, so \(EE_H\) must be applied to the post-lag distribution. (iii) Non-normal MTM (options, path-dependent flows) invalidates the closed form.
Interviewer follow-up: Why does a 1m threshold cut EE from 0.798m (\(H=0\), \(\sigma\varphi(0)=2\times0.399\)) to 0.396m, a reduction of only 0.40m? (The reduction is \(E[\min(V^+,H)]\), which is bounded by \(H\) and here sits well below it because most of the mass lies below the threshold.)

front: Derivation: Basel III final reduced BA-CVA, counterparty capital aggregation. Write the systematic and idiosyncratic components of \(K_{reduced}=\sqrt{\bigl(\rho\sum_c S_c\bigr)^2+(1-\rho^2)\sum_c S_c^2}\) with \(\rho=0.5\) and interpret the two limits. Evaluate for \(S=(10,5,2)\) (in £m of standalone CVA capital inputs).
back:
Steps:
  1. \(K^2=\rho^2(\sum S_c)^2+(1-\rho^2)\sum S_c^2\). Writing it this way shows \(K\) interpolates between two cases.
  2. Limit \(\rho=1\): \(K=\sum S_c\), full correlation (systematic).
  3. Limit \(\rho=0\): \(K=\sqrt{\sum S_c^2}\), no correlation (idiosyncratic).
  4. Evaluate: \(\sum S_c=17\), \(\sum S_c^2=129\). \(K=\sqrt{72.25+96.75}=\sqrt{169}=13.0\).
  5. Bounds: \(11.36\le 13.0\le 17.0\).
Source: \(\rho=50\%\) is the supervisory correlation in the reduced BA-CVA formula (BCBS MAR50; confirmed in vendor documentation of the BA-CVA rules). The discount scalar and the full-BA-CVA weighting between reduced and hedged components are not part of this formula.
Where it breaks: This is the reduced formula only. The full BA-CVA adds a hedge-recognition component with its own parameters, which are not covered here. SA-CVA requires supervisory approval and is not computed by this formula.
Interviewer follow-up: Why does a bank with more counterparties have a lower K per unit of SCVA? (Diversification: the idiosyncratic term grows like the square root of the number of names, the systematic one linearly, so K/ΣS falls as names are added.)

front: Derivation: Vega of a threshold exposure. For \(V\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), \(EE_H(\sigma)=(\mu-H)N(d)+\sigma\varphi(d)\), with \(d=(\mu-H)/\sigma\). Show that \(\partial EE_H/\partial\sigma=\varphi(d)\) and evaluate it for the card with \(\mu=0\), \(\sigma=2\)m, \(H=1\)m.
back:
Steps:
  1. \(\partial d/\partial\sigma=-d/\sigma\). \(N'(d)=\varphi(d)\), \(\varphi'(d)=-d\varphi(d)\).
  2. Term by term: \((\mu-H)\varphi(d)(-d/\sigma)+\varphi(d)+\sigma(-d\varphi(d))(-d/\sigma)\).
  3. Using \(\mu-H=d\sigma\), the first term is \(-d^2\varphi\) and the third is \(+d^2\varphi\). They cancel.
  4. Result: \(\partial EE_H/\partial\sigma=\varphi(d)\). For the example, \(\varphi(-0.5)=0.3521\). A finite-difference check gives 0.35207.
Where it breaks: The identity holds for a normal MTM. With a MTA, the discontinuous collateral makes the vega jump at the MTA boundaries. With a volatility skew, the normal vega is not the right risk measure.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is the vega of a threshold exposure largest when the threshold is near the money? (\(\varphi(d)\) peaks at \(d=0\), i.e. \(H=\mu\), where the density of the MTM at the threshold is largest.)

front: Derivation: Spread CS01 of a flat-hazard CVA. With \(CVA(\lambda)=LGD\cdot EE\cdot\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+r}\bigl(1-e^{-(\lambda+r)T}\bigr)\), \(\lambda=s/LGD\), derive \(\partial CVA/\partial\lambda\) and convert to a per-basis-point spread sensitivity. Evaluate for \(LGD=60\%\), \(EE=3\)m, \(r=3\%\), \(T=5\), \(s=120\)bp.
back:
Steps:
  1. Let \(u=\lambda+r\). \(\partial_\lambda\frac{\lambda}{u}=\frac{r}{u^2}\). \(\partial_\lambda(1-e^{-uT})=Te^{-uT}\).
  2. \(\partial CVA/\partial\lambda=LGD\cdot EE\bigl[\frac{r}{u^2}(1-e^{-uT})+\frac{\lambda}{u}Te^{-uT}\bigr]\).
  3. Evaluate: \(u=0.05\), \(e^{-0.25}=0.7788\). \(\partial CVA/\partial\lambda=1.8\times[0.03/0.0025\times0.2212+0.4\times5\times0.7788]=7.58\)m per unit \(\lambda\). Numerical differentiation agrees.
  4. Per bp of spread: \(\partial s=LGD\,\partial\lambda\), so \(CS01=7.58\times 0.6^{-1}\times10^{-4}=1.26\times10^{-3}\)m, about £1.26k/bp.
Where it breaks: The flat-hazard formula uses one exposure and one hazard. A term-structure CS01 has bucket weights that depend on where EE sits, and the \(\lambda=s/LGD\) step ignores the difference between par and hazard spreads when the curve is steep.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is the CS01 (£1.26k/bp) below the naive ratio \(CVA/(\lambda\,LGD)\) of about £1.33k/bp? (The CVA is concave in \(\lambda\) because survival weighting flattens the response, so the marginal sensitivity is below the average slope from zero.)

front: Case study: Monte Carlo accuracy of expected exposure at one node. Normal MTM \(V\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\), \(\sigma=1\). Compute the EE, the per-path standard deviation of \(V^+\), and the number of paths for a relative standard error of 0.1%.
back:
Steps:
  1. \(EE=\sigma\varphi(0)=0.3989\).
  2. \(\text{sd}(V^+)=\sigma\sqrt{\tfrac12-\tfrac1{2\pi}}=0.5838\).
  3. With 10,000 paths: SE \(=0.5838/\sqrt{10^4}=0.00584\), relative SE \(=1.46\%\).
  4. For a 0.1% relative SE: \(\sqrt N=0.5838/(0.001\times0.3989)=1464\), so \(N\approx2.1\)m paths.
Sanity check: Relative error falls as \(1/\sqrt N\), so a 10x tighter tolerance costs 100x the paths. Path-level errors at neighbouring nodes are highly correlated, so the CVA integral error is not the sum of independent node errors.
Interviewer follow-up: How would you reduce the number of paths needed without biasing EE? (Antithetic variates or control variates using a forward-based exposure with known expectation; the bias comes only from a non-martingale control.)

front: [KVA deeper] A 10-year uncleared swap has a small risk-weighted asset (RWA) because its SA-CCR exposure is largely offset by collateral. Under a binding leverage-ratio constraint, why can its KVA still be large, and what changes in the capital charge?
back:
Answer: The leverage ratio uses an exposure measure (notional-based or SA-CCR-based exposure, without risk weights), not RWA. If the leverage constraint binds, the marginal capital cost of a trade is set by its contribution to the leverage exposure measure, not by its RWA. A trade with low RWA and high leverage exposure can therefore consume leverage capital while showing a small capital charge on the RWA basis.
Desk implication: The KVA charge must use the constraint that binds for the bank, and the capital allocation should be computed on both bases. Using RWA alone can understate the cost of long-dated, collateralised-but-large-notional trades.
Where it breaks: The leverage exposure measure has its own netting and collateral rules, which differ from SA-CCR, so the leverage charge is not simply the RWA charge times a constant.
Interviewer follow-up: Which constraint should you price against? (The one that binds on the marginal trade in the relevant state; in practice a bank can switch between constraints across the life of the trade, which makes KVA state-dependent.)

front: Regulatory: Under Basel III final, why does an internal CVA-desk hedge under SA-CVA count only when the trading desk also executes a matching external trade? Explain the mechanism at the desk level, and say what approval SA-CVA needs.
back:
Mechanism: An external CVA hedge is recognised under SA-CVA if it is eligible (MAR50.37 to 50.39), and eligible hedges leave the market-risk charge. An internal hedge between the CVA desk and the trading desk is two perfectly offsetting internal positions. For curvature, DRC and residual-risk-add-on instruments it counts only if the trading desk also executes an external trade that exactly offsets its position with the CVA desk. This stops a bank recognising an internal hedge that is not backed by an external exposure.
Approval: SA-CVA requires prior supervisory approval. Without it a bank must use the Basic Approach (BA-CVA).
Interviewer follow-up: Does an exact external offset make the hedge economically equivalent to a P&L hedge? (No. Capital recognition is narrower: the desk still carries basis and model risk in the hedge.)

front: Convention: ISDA SIMM initial margin for uncleared derivatives is calibrated to what horizon and confidence level, and how does that choice affect the MPoR used in MVA?
back:
Answer: SIMM is calibrated to a 10-business-day margin period at 99% confidence (ISDA SIMM methodology). Its IM is therefore a 10-day, 99% measure, not a close-out-period measure.
Implication for MVA: The IM you fund is the margin the counterparty requires, not your own close-out exposure. If the MVA model uses a longer funding horizon, the IM must be re-scaled or re-simulated, and the scaling must be justified rather than assumed to be \(\sqrt{t}\).
Interviewer follow-up: Why is a \(\sqrt{t}\) scaling of SIMM IM to a longer horizon an approximation? (Risk-factor returns are not iid over the longer window, and the SIMM correlation matrix and risk weights are fixed for the 10-day calibration.)

front: For a netting set with sensitivities \(s\) and correlation matrix \(R\), the SIMM-style IM \(\sqrt{s^\top R s}\) is homogeneous of degree {{c1::one}} in \(s\). The marginal IM of adding a trade \(a\) is {{c2::\(a^\top R s/\text{IM}\)}}, not the standalone IM of that trade.
back: Euler allocation: \(\partial IM/\partial\varepsilon=a^\top R s/IM\) at \(\varepsilon=0\). Ref: the SIMM chain card 2/3.

front: Under the reduced BA-CVA formula with \(\rho=0.5\), the systematic component is built from {{c1::the sum of the standalone SCVA}} and the idiosyncratic component from {{c2::the square root of the sum of squared SCVA}}.
back: Check with \(S=(10,5,2)\): \(\sqrt{(0.5\cdot17)^2+0.75\cdot129}=13.0\). \(\rho=50\%\) is the supervisory correlation.

front: For \(V\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), the vega of the threshold exposure \(E[(V-H)^+]\) with respect to normal volatility is {{c1::\(\varphi(d)\)}}, where \(d=(\mu-H)/\sigma\).
back: Bachelier identity: the vega of a normal option is the standard normal density at the standardised strike. Here \(\varphi(-0.5)=0.3521\).

front: \(E^{\mathbb Q}[D(0,t)V_t]=\) {{c1::\(P(0,t)\)}} \(\cdot E^{t}[V_t]\), where \(E^t\) is the expectation under the {{c2::\(t\)-forward}} measure with numeraire \(P(\cdot,t)\).
back: Change of numeraire from the spot measure to the \(t\)-forward measure. The pathwise CVA integral still needs one consistent measure across nodes.

front: With a lognormal hazard \(\lambda=\lambda_0 e^{bZ-b^2/2}\), the mean hazard stays {{c1::\(\lambda_0\)}}, because {{c2::\(E[e^{bZ-b^2/2}]=1\)}}.
back: Calibrating the mean hazard to the market isolates the dependence effect from any change in average default probability.
